transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because... I just can't seem to keep my mind on the actual experiment anymore. Like, I'll be on a grant call, or sitting in a safety meeting—which, honestly, those safety meetings are so incredibly redundant, they use the exact same slides from five years ago with this awful yellow font, I keep telling the department head it's unreadable on the projector and nobody absorbs the material—but anyway, I'll be in one of those, and I'll notice a pump vibration through the floor. Or a student will make some random side comment, or I'll just glance over and see this odd peak in an old spectrum from months ago. And suddenly I'm just... I'm off chasing that. For hours and hours. I'll be completely consumed by it, while the actual thing everyone desperately needs from me just completely falls apart.

When you get pulled into investigating one of these anomalies, does it feel like you're anxiously compelled to resolve it because it's bothering you, or more like you're absorbed and genuinely enjoying chasing it, even though you know you should stop?

I'm not really sure if it's anxiety or... or if I'm enjoying it. I haven't really thought about it in those terms. It's more just... well, take the mass spectrometer in the main lab, for instance. We got this new one last year, and the installation tech—Dave, I think his name was, he wore these incredibly bright neon green sneakers that completely violated the closed-toe leather shoe policy, but nobody said anything to him—anyway, he insisted the calibration was perfect. 

But I knew it wasn't. Because if you look at the baseline noise, it's totally different from our old system. And Dave was telling me he used to work in food science, testing the melting point of different commercial cheeses. Which is actually really fascinating when you think about the lipid structures involved. I actually spent a whole weekend reading about dairy polymers after he left because it just blew my mind how complex it is, the way the proteins matrix together. 

But... wait, what were you asking? Oh, right, how the chasing feels. Yeah, I don't really know how to label it. I just sort of end up doing it.

If you deliberately tried to stop yourself and not look into one of these anomalies or side details, would you feel anxious or distressed until you resolved it, or would you just feel bored or unsatisfied?

I don't know if I'd feel anxious, exactly. I mean, I've never really tried to stop myself, to be honest. It's like... well, like the other day, I was supposed to be finalizing this quarterly budget report for the grant renewal. And the spreadsheet they make us use—it's this archaic Excel template from, like, 2012, and the macros are completely broken. I keep telling the admin team they need to migrate to a cloud-based system, but they just look at me like I'm speaking Latin. 

Anyway, I was looking at the equipment depreciation column, and I noticed the centrifuge maintenance log was off by two days. Two days! And I just had to know why. Because if the log is off, maybe the rotor balance is off, and if the rotor balance is off... well, you remember what happened in that lab in Texas a few years ago, right? The whole thing practically exploded. Shrapnel everywhere. I actually met one of the postdocs from that lab at a conference in Denver once. We ended up talking for three hours about the tensile strength of aluminum alloys at high speeds. 

So, I don't know. I guess I don't really try to stop myself, so I couldn't tell you if it makes me distressed or bored. I just sort of... follow the thread.

Aside from getting distracted by these details, do you find it hard to pick up on social cues in conversations—like knowing when to stop talking, or noticing that the other person has lost interest—or to keep a back-and-forth conversation going with colleagues?

I don't think I have a problem with that. I mean, I talk to my colleagues all the time. Actually, just this morning I was talking to Sarah—she's the new lab manager, she just moved here from Boston and she was telling me about how terrible the traffic was on the Mass Pike, which is so true, I drove through there once in 2018 and I swear I didn't move for three hours. And we were talking, and I was explaining my theory about the mass spectrometer baseline noise to her. She seemed really interested, honestly. She was nodding and everything. Though, to be fair, she was also trying to fix the jammed printer at the same time. The printers in our building are an absolute nightmare. It's always a paper jam in tray two, always. I've tried to show them how to load the paper so it doesn't curl, because it's the humidity in the room that warps the fibers, you know? The HVAC system is completely unbalanced. 

But no, I don't think I miss social cues. I'm pretty good at reading people.

Can you tell me whether you've experienced this kind of getting pulled into distracting details and losing track of tasks since you were a child, or is this something that's really only become noticeable in your adult work life?

Oh, no, definitely not since I was a child. When I was a kid, I was actually incredibly focused. I used to build these elaborate model airplanes—the balsa wood kind, you know? My dad and I would spend hours just sanding the wings. He was an aviation mechanic, actually, worked for Delta for thirty years before he retired to Florida. The humidity down there is terrible for his joints, though. I keep telling him he should move out to Arizona, but he loves the ocean too much. He's always sending me pictures of the brown pelicans on his dock. 

But no, this whole... getting pulled into everything and losing track of time, it's pretty recent. It really only started about seven months ago. That's when I took over the multi-site spectroscopy project. Which, honestly, has been a complete logistical nightmare from day one. Coordinating between the Chicago lab and our facility here is like trying to herd cats. The Chicago team insists on using this proprietary software for their data logging, and it doesn't interface with our open-source system at all. I had to call their IT guy, Greg, and we were on the phone for two hours trying to write a custom patch. Greg collects vintage fountain pens, by the way, which I didn't even know was a thing, but he showed me this 1920s Waterman pen on Zoom and the gold nib was just... it was a literal work of art. The way the capillary action works in those old ink feeds is fascinating, I ended up looking up fluid dynamics in vintage pens for the rest of the afternoon. 

But yeah, about seven months. Right when that project started.
Over these past seven months, have you also noticed feeling unusually elated, irritable, or full of energy, or needing much less sleep than usual, alongside this distractibility?

Well, electrified is a good word for it. Honestly, for months now, I've felt like... like the whole lab is finally moving at my speed, you know? It's like I'm completely charged up, and I don't even need coffee anymore. I used to drink three cups of French roast before noon, the dark roast from that little place down on 4th Street. They roast their own beans right in the shop, and the smell when you walk in is just incredible. The owner, Marcus, he was telling me about how the roasting temperature affects the acidity of the beans, which is actually a really interesting chemical process when you break it down. 

But yeah, I just feel so energized. Though, I guess... well, it's great until someone gets in my way. Like, if one of the grad students questions my plan or tells me I need to slow down, I just snap. I don't mean to, but it's like they're moving in slow motion and it's so frustrating. I kind of went off on one of the second-years last week because he couldn't keep up with the new protocol I wrote, and now I've noticed the students are basically avoiding my office. Which is fine, honestly, because I get more done without them interrupting me to ask where the spare pipettes are. Like, they're in the drawer labeled 'pipettes,' it's not a mystery. We use the P200s for almost everything anyway, and the manufacturer just changed the plastic they use for the tips, which is supposed to be more eco-friendly, but I swear the surface tension is different now. I was actually going to run a quick test on the new tips this afternoon to see if it affects the volume calibration.
Over these past seven months, have you noticed needing much less sleep than you used to—say only a few hours a night—while still feeling rested and full of energy the next day?

Honestly, sleep just feels like an inefficient interruption at this point. I mean, why lie in bed doing nothing when my brain is completely ready to go? Most nights I'm only sleeping two, maybe three hours tops. I usually just end up passing out on the couch with my laptop still open on my chest. I finally upgraded to one of the new laptops with the ARM-based processors, and let me tell you, the thermal efficiency is incredible. It doesn't even get hot on my legs like the old ones did. My old Dell used to sound like a literal jet engine taking off just trying to run a basic Python script, and the fan would blow this hot, dusty air everywhere. Dust is actually a huge problem for electronics, it insulates the components and causes thermal throttling, which degrades the silicon over time. I try to tell the IT department we need better air purifiers in the server room, but they never listen. 

But anyway, yeah, I'll wake up at like 3 AM on the couch, and I'm instantly sharp. Completely rested and ready to get right back to work. I just open my eyes and start typing again, not tired at all. The streetlights outside my living room window are those new bright white LEDs the city installed last fall, which is terrible for light pollution—they scatter so much more in the atmosphere than the old orange high-pressure sodium lamps, the Rayleigh scattering is just off the charts—but it gives me enough light to see my keyboard without turning on a lamp, so I guess it works out. But yeah, just a few hours is plenty for me right now.

Before these past seven months, have you ever had a period—lasting days or weeks—where you felt unusually depressed, low, or lost interest in things, or on the flip side, an earlier time when you felt this same kind of high energy and reduced need for sleep?

Well, honestly, I've never really been the depressed type. You know, lying around, not wanting to do anything? That just isn't me. Even when things get tough, I usually just dive into my work. Though, speaking of diving, I did try scuba diving once when I was in my twenties, down in Cozumel. The reef there is absolutely stunning, the colors of the parrotfish are just surreal. Did you know they actually secrete a mucus cocoon around themselves at night to hide their scent from predators? It's a fascinating biological adaptation, really. It's like a tiny, transparent sleeping bag made of slime. I read this whole paper on the chemical composition of it once, it has these specific glycoproteins... 

But wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling low or whatever. No, I haven't really had anything like that. And as for this kind of energy, this feeling of being totally plugged in and not needing sleep? No, this is definitely a first. Like I said, it just kicked into high gear about seven months ago with that spectroscopy project. Before that, I was just... normal, I guess. I mean, I always worked hard, but I definitely needed my solid seven hours of sleep. I used to have this whole nighttime routine with chamomile tea and a book. I read a lot of historical non-fiction. I was reading this huge biography of Catherine the Great right before all this started. She was actually an incredible patron of the arts, she basically started the Hermitage Museum collection. She bought this entire collection of paintings from a Berlin merchant just to show off to Frederick the Great. The politics of art acquisition in the 18th century were just vicious... but yeah, no, I've never felt this kind of constant, buzzing energy before now.

Which is fine, honestly, because I get more done without them interrupting me to ask where the spare pipettes are. Like, they're in the drawer labeled 'pipettes,' it's not a mystery. We use the P200s for almost everything anyway, and the manufacturer just changed the plastic they use for the tips, which is supposed to be more eco-friendly, but I swear the surface tension is different now. I was actually going to run a quick test on the new tips this afternoon to see if it affects the volume calibration.

inference.note: The patient now endorses clear hypomanic/manic features—subjective sense of being 'electrified,' markedly increased energy with reduced need for stimulants, irritability with snapping at students, and grandiose-tinged behavior—alongside the distractibility. This pattern, emerging acutely 7 months ago without childhood history, is best explained by a manic episode rather than an organic cognitive or personality change, so F06.7 and F06.8 are ruled out.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has been sleeping significantly less than usual over these seven months without feeling tired, a core manic symptom
doctor.question: Over these past seven months, have you noticed needing much less sleep than you used to—say only a few hours a night—while still feeling rested and full of energy the next day?

target_item.name: Decreased_Sleep
target_item.manifestation: Most nights I sleep two or three hours, sometimes on the couch with my laptop open, and I wake up sharp and ready to work instead of tired, like sleep is an inefficient interruption.
target_item.reason: The doctor is explicitly asking if I need less sleep than usual (only a few hours) and still feel rested and full of energy, which matches the Decreased_Sleep symptom.

patient.answer:
Honestly, sleep just feels like an inefficient interruption at this point. I mean, why lie in bed doing nothing when my brain is completely ready to go? Most nights I'm only sleeping two, maybe three hours tops. I usually just end up passing out on the couch with my laptop still open on my chest. I finally upgraded to one of the new laptops with the ARM-based processors, and let me tell you, the thermal efficiency is incredible. It doesn't even get hot on my legs like the old ones did. My old Dell used to sound like a literal jet engine taking off just trying to run a basic Python script, and the fan would blow this hot, dusty air everywhere. Dust is actually a huge problem for electronics, it insulates the components and causes thermal throttling, which degrades the silicon over time. I try to tell the IT department we need better air purifiers in the server room, but they never listen. 

But anyway, yeah, I'll wake up at like 3 AM on the couch, and I'm instantly sharp. Completely rested and ready to get right back to work. I just open my eyes and start typing again, not tired at all. The streetlights outside my living room window are those new bright white LEDs the city installed last fall, which is terrible for light pollution—they scatter so much more in the atmosphere than the old orange high-pressure sodium lamps, the Rayleigh scattering is just off the charts—but it gives me enough light to see my keyboard without turning on a lamp, so I guess it works out. But yeah, just a few hours is plenty for me right now.

inference.note: Patient now endorses full manic syndrome (marked decreased need for sleep with subjective wellness, elevated/irritable mood, grandiose overconfidence in his judgment, increased goal-directed activity, distractibility) that began abruptly 7 months ago with no childhood history of inattention—this rules out ADHD-type distractibility and supports a discrete manic episode. Absence of psychotic features narrows from broad F30.8 to F30.1; F31.1 remains possible if a prior depressive episode is later identified, making this bipolar I rather than a single manic episode.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this is a first-ever mood episode or part of a recurring pattern, to distinguish a single manic episode from bipolar disorder
doctor.question: Before these past seven months, have you ever had a period—lasting days or weeks—where you felt unusually depressed, low, or lost interest in things, or on the flip side, an earlier time when you felt this same kind of high energy and reduced need for sleep?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of depressive episodes or prior manic episodes before the current 7-month period, which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, honestly, I've never really been the depressed type. You know, lying around, not wanting to do anything? That just isn't me. Even when things get tough, I usually just dive into my work. Though, speaking of diving, I did try scuba diving once when I was in my twenties, down in Cozumel. The reef there is absolutely stunning, the colors of the parrotfish are just surreal. Did you know they actually secrete a mucus cocoon around themselves at night to hide their scent from predators? It's a fascinating biological adaptation, really. It's like a tiny, transparent sleeping bag made of slime. I read this whole paper on the chemical composition of it once, it has these specific glycoproteins... 

But wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling low or whatever. No, I haven't really had anything like that. And as for this kind of energy, this feeling of being totally plugged in and not needing sleep? No, this is definitely a first. Like I said, it just kicked into high gear about seven months ago with that spectroscopy project. Before that, I was just... normal, I guess. I mean, I always worked hard, but I definitely needed my solid seven hours of sleep. I used to have this whole nighttime routine with chamomile tea and a book. I read a lot of historical non-fiction. I was reading this huge biography of Catherine the Great right before all this started. She was actually an incredible patron of the arts, she basically started the Hermitage Museum collection. She bought this entire collection of paintings from a Berlin merchant just to show off to Frederick the Great. The politics of art acquisition in the 18th century were just vicious... but yeah, no, I've never felt this kind of constant, buzzing energy before now.

inference.note: Patient denies any prior depressive or manic episodes before the past 7 months, ruling out a bipolar course (F31.1). Current presentation shows clear manic symptoms (elevated/irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, distractibility, tangential speech, increased goal-directed activity) consistent with a single manic episode (F30.1).

opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a first-ever, distinct episode lasting 7 months characterized by elevated, expansive, and irritable mood ('electrified,' 'plugged in'), decreased need for sleep (2-3 hours with full restoration), increased distractibility, excessive involvement in tangential activities, irritability with poor judgment leading to interpersonal conflict, and grandiose certainty in professional judgment. There is no history of prior depressive or manic episodes, ruling out Bipolar I (recurrent, F31.1). Symptoms are not present since childhood and do not reflect a lifelong pattern of inattention/hyperactivity independent of mood change, arguing against ADHD (F90.0). No psychotic features (hallucinations/delusions) are reported, supporting mania without psychotic symptoms rather than F30.2. The presentation is a single manic episode, consistent with F30.1.
